opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think it comes pretty naturally out of how open-source communities work. A lot of the people in our developer meetings have never met in person. They're spread across time zones, so for some it's early morning and for others it's midnight. Some are students joining from a dorm room, some are engineers at big companies, some are contributing on their own time. Asking everyone to turn on a camera adds friction, and in open source you want to remove as much friction as possible so people actually show up.

Also, the meeting isn't really about seeing each other's faces. It's about the work. Usually someone shares a screen with a design doc, a benchmark result, or a PR, and everyone's attention is on that. What matters is whether the idea is good, whether the numbers hold up, and who's going to take the next step. Having cameras off actually keeps the focus there.

I also think it lowers the barrier for people who are newer or a bit shy. If you're a first-time contributor and you just want to listen and understand how the project works, being able to join quietly without being on camera makes it much easier. Over time those people start speaking up, then sending PRs, and some become core maintainers. So I don't see it as a lack of engagement. It's more that the real engagement happens in the code, on GitHub, and in Slack, and the meeting is just one piece of that.

That said, when we do get to meet in person, at a conference or a meetup, it's really fun. You finally connect a face to a GitHub handle you've been working with for months, and it feels like meeting an old friend.

r001.rationale: The candidate attributes cameras-off to reducing friction, time-zone constraints, keeping attention on the work, and lowering barriers for newcomers. It does not say that turning cameras on simply does not occur to developers.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it started as a small practical thing and then became a kind of culture. When you're running a project like SGLang, a lot of the people in the meeting are not colleagues in the traditional sense. They're contributors from different companies, different time zones, grad students joining from a lab at midnight, someone dialing in from a café. Nobody wants to be judged on whether they have a nice background or whether they just woke up. Turning the camera off removes that friction, and it lowers the bar for people to just show up.

The other part is that most of our meetings aren't really about people, they're about the thing on the screen. Someone is sharing a PR, a benchmark chart, a profiler trace, and everyone is staring at that. The face in the corner adds very little. In a sense, the code is the face. You get to know people through how they write, how they review, what they care about in a design discussion. I know contributors I've worked with for over a year whose faces I've basically never seen, and I feel I know them quite well.

I also think it's a way of being honest about attention. If my camera is on, I'm performing attention, nodding at the right moments. If it's off, I can actually be reading the diff while someone is talking, and then say something useful when it's my turn. For a very technical group that's a better trade.

That said, I don't think it's a rule we should be proud of in an absolute way. When something is sensitive, like a disagreement about direction or a conversation with a new maintainer who's nervous, I'll turn my camera on, and usually the other person does too. So the habit is really "default off, on when it matters," and I think that's the right balance for an open-source, globally distributed team.

r001.rationale: The candidate gives deliberate reasons for keeping cameras off—reducing social friction, focusing on shared technical material, and avoiding performative attention. It does not say that turning cameras on simply does not occur to developers.

astra-6.text:
I tend to see it as a working preference rather than a sign that people aren’t engaged. In a developer meeting, the shared screen—the code, the logs, the design document—is often where everyone’s attention needs to be. Having your camera on can feel like an extra demand without adding much to that discussion.

But it depends on the meeting. If we’re getting to know someone or having a sensitive conversation, seeing each other can help. For routine technical discussions, I’d pay more attention to whether people ask questions, contribute ideas, and follow through than whether their cameras are on.

r001.rationale: The candidate frames cameras-off as a working preference and says cameras can feel like an extra demand, but does not say developers leave them off because turning them on does not occur to them.

sol-6.1.text: I think it reflects how developers often prefer to work: focusing on the substance of the discussion without necessarily needing to be on camera. If we’re looking at code or sharing a screen, that’s where our attention is anyway. Having the camera off doesn’t necessarily mean someone is disengaged. I’d pay more attention to whether they’re asking questions, contributing ideas, and following through afterward. At the same time, when you’re meeting someone new or having a more personal conversation, turning cameras on can help build a connection.

r001.rationale: The response attributes cameras-off behavior to focusing on discussion or shared code and says it does not imply disengagement. It does not say developers leave cameras off because turning them on does not occur to them.
